chapter_theme: Wealth that is neither enjoyed nor given is effectively no wealth. It does nothing for the holder, the needy or the holder's heirs, and it turns a person into something the world doesn't want. The chapter measures wealth entirely by its use.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: no use to the one who amassed it (1001), no use to others (1002-1004), both failings together (1005-1006), and the faults of such wealth (1007-1010).

1001.reading: One who has stored up great wealth to the brim and doesn't eat it, is dead: there is nothing left for him to do.
1001.nuance: உண்ணான், 'doesn't eat', treats wealth as food. Parimelazhagar widens it to the five senses.

positions.position: The man who does not use it is himself dead, and has nothing further to do with it.
positions.quote: அதனை நுகரானாயின், செத்தான்; அவன் பின்பு செய்யக்கிடந்தது யாது மில்லை.

positions.position: An alternative he allows: once dead, one has no right over it, so enjoy it as soon as it comes.
It is about a literal death: what good is the wealth to one who dies without enjoying it?

1002.reading: Through the delusion of clinging without giving, thinking all things come by wealth, comes a மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
1002.nuance: The delusion isn't the belief that wealth achieves everything, a point the Kural makes elsewhere: it lies in clinging while holding that belief.

positions.position: It means rebirth as a ghost that hungers amid food, matching those who watched others' hunger amid plenty.
It describes a person: he becomes a low being with no distinction, with no rebirth involved.

1003.reading: The appearance on earth of men who cling to accumulation and don't want renown is a burden to the land.
1003.nuance: Parimelazhagar identifies the renown with virtue achieved by giving, so the choice isn't between wealth and vanity. Manakkudavar draws the harshest conclusion: it would be better if they hadn't been born.

1004.reading: What does one wanted by no one imagine will remain behind him?
1004.nuance: The issue is what survives a person, and the question implies nothing does, since fame only rests on givers. Pope's gloss moves this to 'the world to come' while his couplet does not. The Tamil says எச்சம், what is left behind.

1005.reading: Those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, even with crores upon crores.
1005.nuance: An ownership paradox: possession is defined by use. Parimelazhagar says giving is named first because virtue outranks pleasure. Kalaignar fuses the two: those not happy in giving.

1006.reading: One who doesn't use it himself and doesn't naturally give any of it to the deserving is a misfortune with great wealth.

positions.position: The man is a disease of the wealth, which could have done both things.
positions.quote: இரண்டும் செய்தற்கு இடனுடைத்தாய செல்வத்திற்கு ஒரு நோய்.

positions.position: The great wealth obtained by such a person is itself faulty.

1007.reading: The wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is like a woman of exceeding beauty growing old alone.
1007.nuance: The simile mourns what is wasted, and treats a woman's worth as realized through a husband. Parimelazhagar's gloss deepens it: she is unmarried for want of anyone to give her away, a giver being missing in both halves, and she herself loses something too.

1008.reading: The wealth of one who isn't wanted is a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of town.
1008.nuance: நச்சப்படாதவன், 'unwanted', and நச்சு, 'poison', chime, and it is what makes the verse work. Being close by is what makes it worse: Parimelazhagar says he is near the needy and still gives nothing. Manakkudavar extends it, saying any who eat out of desire will die.

1009.reading: Others will take the bright wealth amassed by giving up love, by self-denial and by ignoring virtue.
1009.nuance: The list gives three prices paid, and the last word takes away the prize. Parimelazhagar says பிறர் excludes even his own line. Kalaignar makes ignoring virtue into unethical earning, which is a different charge from not giving.

1010.reading: The சிறுதுனி of the renowned rich has the nature of rain-clouds going dry.
1010.nuance: As a closing verse it gives the positive pole of the chapter's whole contrast: the wealth that does give.

positions.position: சிறுதுனி is brief poverty: those who gave everything soon recover, like a cloud. He rejects the other reading as not suited to this chapter.
சிறுதுனி is slight displeasure that stops their giving, and the world suffers as with failed rain.
positions.quote: சீருடைய செல்வர் சிறுதுனியால் ஈயாதொழிதல், மாரி பெய் யாமை மிக்காற் போலும்

links.note: An exact counter-image. 216: wealth in the hands of the kind is a useful tree fruiting in the village. 1008: wealth in the hands of the unwanted is a poison tree fruiting mid-town. Same setting, same act of fruiting, and the holder's character decides whether it feeds or kills.
214 places one who doesn't do what's fitting 'among the dead', and 1001 calls one who won't use his wealth 'dead'. Both use death as a civil status, assigned for failure to circulate wealth.

211 says that duty seeks no return, as with rain. 1010 extends the identification of generous wealth with rain: even their failures are like clouds running dry. The comparison is a consistent one in the Kural.

அடுக்கிய கோடி recurs. For the well-born in 954, stacked crores cannot buy a lowering act. For the miser in 1005, they amount to nothing. The same sum measures character in one and its absence in the other.

570 says that a harsh sceptre over the unlearned is the only burden on the earth. 1003 uses the same phrase for hoarders. The same claim to being earth's one burden is made against a tyrant and against a hoarder.
233 says nothing is imperishable but high fame, and 1004 asks what the unwanted hoarder imagines will remain. Parimelazhagar's note supplies the link: fame rests only on the giver.

source_issues: 1001: Parimelazhagar's text is truncated at the start, with only the last words of the verse's gloss present.
1002: Pope's gloss has 'will be born a demon' from Parimelazhagar; the verse says மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
1004: Pope's gloss has 'in the world to come', which doesn't match the Tamil எச்சம் or his own couplet.
1007: Kalaignar's text has a stray character after ஒருத்தி.
